title: Longest Common Prefix
interviewTips: Ask if strs can be empty, contain empty strings, or have different lengths and character sets - determines early exits and bounds checks.
Trade-off: vertical scan is O(S) time with O(1) extra space and early exit, sorting is shortest code but pays sort cost, Trie pays extra space but is ideal for many queries on same set.
Edge-case tip: answer can be empty string, single string returns itself, and always check index bounds before charAt access to avoid out-of-bounds.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Vertical Scanning
approaches.intuition: If all strings share a prefix, then every string must have the same character at each prefix position. Check column by column using the first string as reference and stop at first mismatch.
approaches.theory: Let first string be reference of length m and n be number of strings. For column i, compare strs[0][i] against strs[j][i] for all j. If any j is too short or differs, prefix must end before i, so strs[0][:i] is the longest possible. If all columns of first string pass, first string itself is the prefix. This is correct because mismatch at i proves no longer prefix can be common, and no mismatch proves full first string is common.

timeComplexity.explanation: n is number of strings, m is length of shortest string. In worst case compare every character of every string up to m. Early exit on mismatch makes it fast in practice.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only indices and one char variable besides output substring. No extra data structure proportional to input.

steps: reference = flower, i=0 char f: flow[0]=f, flight[0]=f -> continue
i=1 char l: flow[1]=l, flight[1]=l -> continue
i=2 char o: flow[2]=o, flight[2]=i -> mismatch at flight, return flower[:2]

edgeCases: Contains empty string ['', 'abc'] -> return empty string
No common prefix ['dog','racecar','car'] -> return empty string
Different lengths where shortest is prefix ['ab','aba','abc'] -> return ab

approaches.name: Approach 2: Sorting First and Last
approaches.intuition: After lexicographic sorting, the most different strings become first and last. Any prefix common to all must be common to these two extremes, so only compare those two.
approaches.theory: Lexicographic order groups strings by prefix. For any three sorted strings a <= b <= c, if a and c agree on first k chars, b must also agree because its prefix is lexicographically between them. Therefore LCP of whole set equals LCP of min and max strings. Comparing only those two yields answer. Sorting dominates cost.

timeComplexity.explanation: Sorting n strings costs O(n log n) comparisons each up to O(m) char compares, plus O(m) to compare first and last. Concise but slower than vertical scan for large n.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only indices besides sort. Python Timsort and C++ introsort use O(log n) to O(n) auxiliary space depending on implementation, Java Dual-Pivot uses O(log n) stack.

steps: compare: f==f, l==l, i==o mismatch at index 2 -> stop

edgeCases: One empty after sort ['', 'a','b'] -> first is empty -> return empty
Single element -> first==last -> return that string

approaches.name: Approach 3: Trie Prefix Walk
approaches.intuition: Insert all strings into a Trie where each edge is a character. The longest common prefix is the deepest path from root that is shared by all strings with no branching.
approaches.theory: Trie merges common prefixes into shared nodes. Insert each string marking end-of-word. Then walk from root: while current node has exactly one child and is not end of any word and child is shared by all n strings, advance and append char. Stop at branch or word end because that indicates divergence or one string ended. Path collected is LCP.

timeComplexity.explanation: S is total characters across all strings. Each char inserted once and prefix walk is at most O(m). Best when many queries reuse Trie, otherwise overhead vs scan.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Trie stores every character node in worst case with no sharing, plus hashmap overhead per node.

steps: insert all: root->f->l shared, then branch o vs i
walk: f has 1 child, not end -> take f
l has 1 child, not end -> take l
next node has 2 children o and i -> stop

edgeCases: Empty string in input -> Trie root child walk still returns empty due to early return
Single string ['abc'] -> no branching, walk full string -> return abc
Duplicate strings -> is_end stops correctly at shortest end
No common prefix -> root has multiple children -> return empty
